learn.title: The smallest useful program
learn.body: Almost every programmer starts with a program that prints a greeting. It is short, but it contains the pieces every C program needs. Today we read it line by line.

learn.title: hello.c
learn.body: This is the whole program. It prints one line of text.

learn.title: The first line
learn.body: The `#include` line asks the compiler to bring in stdio, the standard input and output library. Without it, the compiler does not know what `printf` is.

learn.title: main
learn.body: `int main(void)` is where every C program starts. Its body sits between the curly braces `{` and `}`. The computer runs the lines inside, in order, from top to bottom.

learn.title: printf and return
learn.body: `printf` prints text. The text goes in double quotes, and the `\n` inside means a new line. Each instruction ends with a semicolon. `return 0;` says the program finished normally.

learn.title: What happens when it runs
learn.body: The computer reads `main` from top to bottom.
steps: It enters `main` at the opening brace
`printf` prints hello, world and then moves to a new line

learn.body: Missing semicolons are the most common beginner mistake. End every instruction with `;`.

questions.prompt: Where does every C program start running?
questions.explanation: The computer begins at `main` and works through its body in order.
`\n` is not printed as letters. It means move to a new line.

questions.prompt: Every instruction in C ends with a \_\_.
questions.explanation: The semicolon marks the end of each instruction.

questions.prompt: The `#include` line for stdio is needed so the compiler knows about \_\_.
questions.explanation: `printf` is declared in the standard input and output library.

questions.prompt: What visible text does `printf("hello, world\n");` print? Type it.
questions.explanation: The text between the quotes is printed. The `\n` only moves to a new line.

questions.prompt: Put these lines of hello.c in order.
questions.explanation: The include comes first, then main, then its body inside braces.
Returning 0 from `main` is the usual way to say everything went fine.
